title: Async JavaScript & APIs
description: Master asynchronous JavaScript — the skill that separates beginners from job-ready developers. Understand the event loop, Promises, async/await, the Fetch API, error handling patterns, and how to build real applications that talk to REST APIs.
learningObjectives: Explain the event loop: call stack, task queue, microtask queue
Write clean async/await code with proper error handling
Fetch data from REST APIs and handle responses
Use Promise.all, Promise.race, and other combinators

sections.content: JavaScript is single-threaded — it has one call stack and processes one thing at a time. Yet it handles network requests, timers, and user events without freezing. The secret: the event loop.
💡 The microtask queue (Promises, queueMicrotask) always drains completely before the task queue (setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events) gets a turn.

exercises.question: In what order do these lines print? console.log('A'); setTimeout(()=>console.log('B'),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log('C')); console.log('D');
hints: Synchronous first, then microtasks, then macrotasks
exercises.explanation: A and D are synchronous. C is a microtask (Promise.then) — runs after synchronous code. B is a macrotask (setTimeout) — runs last. Order: A → D → C → B.

exercises.question: You have 3 independent API calls. You want ALL of them to succeed before proceeding. Which combinator should you use?
exercises.explanation: Promise.all() runs all promises in parallel and resolves when all succeed. If any one fails, it rejects immediately. Use Promise.allSettled() if you want to inspect the result of each, regardless of success/failure.

sections.content: Writing Async Code That Reads Like Sync

exercises.question: What does the async keyword do to a function's return value?
options: Wraps the return value in a Promise
exercises.correctAnswer: Wraps the return value in a Promise
hints: async functions always return a Promise
exercises.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise. If you return 'hello', the caller gets Promise.resolve('hello'). If you throw an error, the caller gets a rejected Promise.

sections.content: ⚠️ fetch() only throws on network failure — not on HTTP errors (4xx, 5xx). Always check response.ok or response.status explicitly.

exercises.question: fetch('/api/data') rejects (throws) when:
options: There is a network error (no connection)
exercises.correctAnswer: There is a network error (no connection)
hints: HTTP errors are not the same as network errors
exercises.explanation: fetch() only rejects on network-level failures (server unreachable, DNS failure, CORS block). HTTP errors like 404 and 500 resolve successfully — you must check response.ok to detect them.

exercises.question: What is exponential backoff in retry logic?
options: Increasing the wait time between retries exponentially (100ms, 200ms, 400ms...)
Reducing the request payload size on each retry
Splitting the request into smaller chunks
exercises.correctAnswer: Increasing the wait time between retries exponentially (100ms, 200ms, 400ms...)
hints: Each retry waits longer than the last
exercises.explanation: Exponential backoff increases delay between retries by a factor (like 2x) each time. This prevents overwhelming a struggling server with rapid retries and is standard practice for production APIs.

capstoneProject.title: Weather Dashboard
capstoneProject.description: Build a fully functional weather dashboard that fetches live data from the OpenWeatherMap API.
requirements: Search input with debouncing using setTimeout
apiFetch wrapper with custom ApiError classes
5-day forecast using Promise.all to fetch multiple endpoints in parallel
AbortController cancels in-flight requests when a new search starts
Retry logic with exponential backoff for failed requests
localStorage caches successful responses for 10 minutes
Use IntersectionObserver to animate forecast cards on scroll
Comprehensive error UI for network errors, 404, and rate limit errors
